extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students in philosophy/history/sociology of science (philosophers of science, historians of science, sociologists of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and characterizing the standards, components, and procedural criteria by which scientific communities, paradigms (disciplinary matrices), crises, and revolutions are identified and evaluated. Focuses on what a paradigm/disciplinary matrix contains, how communities are delimited, and what counts as crisis/revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying a scientific community
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific community consists of the practitioners of a scientific specialty who have undergone similar education and professional initiation, absorbed the same technical literature, and taken responsibility for a shared set of goals including training successors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community membership is ordinarily established by subject matter boundaries marked by standard literature, membership in professional societies, journals read, attendance at special conferences, distribution of draft manuscripts/galley proofs, and formal/informal communication networks (e.g., correspondence and citation linkages). Communities may be of varying size (perhaps ~100 members or fewer) and individuals may belong to multiple communities. Identification of communities is a prerequisite to locating paradigms and analyzing normal science vs revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangling 'paradigm' from community structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid circularity: a paradigm is what members of a scientific community share while a community consists of those who share a paradigm. Communities should be isolated empirically first; paradigms can then be discovered by scrutinizing members' behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The postscript recommends isolating communities by empirical techniques (conferences, citation networks, societies) before attributing a paradigm, to reduce conceptual circularity. This analytic separation clarifies many apparent problems in the original treatment of paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary matrix as replacement analytic concept for 'paradigm' (global sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'disciplinary matrix' to denote the whole constellation of ordered elements (beliefs, values, techniques, etc.) shared by a discipline's practitioners, instead of the ambiguous global use of 'paradigm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disciplinary matrix is composed of different sorts of components (symbolic generalizations, models, values, exemplars) that function together but are not all of a piece; separating them aids analysis of scientific practice and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of symbolic generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic generalizations are the formal or readily formalizable expressions (e.g., f = ma, I = V/R) that group members deploy without question; they function both as laws and, to an extent, as definitions of the symbols they use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These generalizations enable logical and mathematical manipulation in puzzle-solving. Their acceptance can increase a science's power, may require redefinition of terms (e.g., Ohm’s Law demanding redefinition of 'current' and 'resistance'), and revolutions often involve abandoning generalizations whose force was partly tautological. Examples: Joule–Lenz Law (functioned mainly as law), Ohm’s Law (had definitional force and encountered resistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of models (heuristic and ontological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared commitments to particular models (e.g., heat as kinetic energy; molecules as elastic billiard balls; electric circuit as hydrodynamic analog) provide preferred analogies and metaphors, help determine acceptable explanations and puzzle-solutions, and help identify unsolved puzzles and their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models vary in strength from heuristic to ontological; membership in a community may not require commitment to a given model (e.g., early 19th-century chemists could work effectively without believing in atoms). Models guide what counts as an explanation and shape research agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared values guiding scientific practice and theory choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Values commonly shared by scientists include: predictions should be accurate; quantitative predictions are preferable to qualitative; margins of permissible error should be consistently satisfied; theories should permit puzzle-formulation and solution; they should be simple, self-consistent, plausible, and compatible with other deployed theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values are more widely shared across communities than symbolic generalizations or specific models but are applied variably by individuals. Variable application is important: it distributes risk, allows conservative resolution of most anomalies by normal means, and permits some practitioners to take high-risk moves that can lead to revolutions. Values therefore guide judgments of anomaly, crisis, and theory choice but do not determine unique outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as exemplars / puzzle-solutions (second, narrower sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the narrower sense, a paradigm denotes concrete puzzle-solutions or exemplary past achievements used as models by practitioners to guide the solution of remaining puzzles, effectively replacing explicit rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sense is philosophically deeper and is the source of controversies about subjectivity and incommensurability; such exemplars embody tacit knowledge not easily paraphrased as explicit rules but are systematic, time-tested, and corrigible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and identification of crises and revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A revolution is a special sort of change involving reconstruction of group commitments; it need not be large and may occur within small communities (perhaps fewer than 25 people). Crisis (the common awareness that something has gone wrong) is a usual prelude to revolution but not an absolute prerequisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crises supply a self-correcting mechanism ensuring normal science’s rigidity is checked; revolutions may also be induced by developments external to the affected community (e.g., new instruments or laws from another specialty). Analysts should not equate revolution size with historical prominence—many revolutions are small-scale but significant within their communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological implication: locate group(s) before studying paradigms or revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of paradigm-directed or paradigm-shattering research must begin by locating the responsible group(s) rather than assuming paradigms correspond one-to-one with subject matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical subjects often shift community boundaries over time (e.g., 'physics' formed by merging parts of mathematics and natural philosophy); theories that appear to lack unanimity may reflect cross-community tool usage rather than intra-community disagreement. Correctly locating communities dissolves many apparent counterexamples to paradigm-unanimity claims.
